la:verb:struo.gloss: to place one thing on top of another, to pile up, join together
senses: to place one thing on top of another, to pile up, join together
to ready, prepare, devise, design, contrive, arrange, plot, aim at, accomplish, to make or do a plan, purpose, intent, or course of action
la:verb:struo.html:
strŭo, xi, ctum, 3, v. a.
root στορ; Gr. στρώννυμι, to spread; cf. Sanscr. upa-star, to make ready; and v. sterno
,
to place by or upon each other; to pile up, arrange, etc.
Lit.
In gen. (rare but class.; cf. condo, compono): quasi structa et nexa verbis, etc.,: lateres, qui super musculo struantur,: altaque congestos struxisse ad sidera montes,: arbores in pyram,: frugem ordine,: avenas,: ordine longo penum,; ; hence, poet., transf.: altaria donis,: acervum,: congeriem armorum,: opes, rem,to heap up, accumulate,; : PEDEM, to heap up steps, i. e. to flee: SI CALVITVR PEDEMVE STRVIT MANVM ENDOIACITO, Fragm. XII. Tab. ap. Müll.—Absol.: aliae (apes) struunt, aliae poliunt, aliae suggerunt, pile up (the comb), . —
In partic.
To make by joining together; to build, erect, fabricate, make, form, construct (syn. aedifico): fornacem bene struito ... lateribus summam (fornacem) struito, and 3: per speluncas saxis structas, Poët. ap. (Trag. Rel. p. 208 Rib.); imitated by ; cf.: templa saxo structa vetusto,: moenia saxo,: moenia,: domos,: pyras,: ingentem pyram,; : navem,: tubas,to make,cubilia,: convivia,to get ready, prepare, et saep.— Absol.: reticulata structura, quā frequentissime Romae struunt,. —Part. perf., subst.: saxorum structa,masonry,.—
With the idea of order predominating, to set in order, arrange: copias ante frontem castrorum struit,arranges, draws up in rank and file,; so, aciem,; ; : omnes armatos in campo, Liv 42, 51.—
Trop.
In gen., to join together, compound, compose: ex praepositione et duobus vocabulis dure videtur struxisse Pacuvius, Nerei repandirostrum,.—
In partic.
To prepare something detrimental; to cause, occasion; to devise, contrive, instigate, etc. (very freq., esp. in Cic.): struunt sorores Atticae dirum nefas, Poët. ap. Mar. Vict. p. 2596 P. (Trag. Rel. p. 272 Rib.): aliquid calamitatis struere et moliri,: sycophantias,: num me fefellit hosce id struere?: sollicitudinem sibi,: odium in alios,: insidias alicui,: consilia recuperandi regni,; ; : periculum ruinae, Caecin. ap. : pericula alicui,: mortem alicui,: crimina et accusatores,; cf.: ultroque struebantur qui monerent perfugere ad Germaniae exercilus,

: controversiam de nomine,: causas,: quid struit?: quid struis?; .—

To order, arrange, dispose, regulate: rem domi,: verba,: bene structa collocatio,: orationem,: orationem solutam, Prob. ap. : dum proxima dicimus, struere ulteriora possimus,: quid parum structum (in oratione),: cum varios struerem per saecula reges,ordained,.—
To fit out, provide with (late Lat.): quot steriles utriusque naturae infructuosis genitalibus structi,: sermo autem spiritu structus est,; .—Hence, structē, adv., orderly, regularly, methodically (very rare): historiam scripsere Sallustius structe, Pictor incondite,: quae nobis causa est structius prodeundi?with more embellishment, more ornately,.

la:noun:strues.html:
strŭes, is, f.
id.
,
a heap, pile of things put together.
In gen. (class.; syn.: acervus, cumulus, congeries): laterum,: corporum,; ; : lignorum,; : arma cum telis in strue mixta,: rogi,a funeral pile, pyre,; ; ; : uvarum, et saep.: (milites Macedones) confusa strue implicantur,a heap, mass, phalanx,.—Collect., with a verb in the plur.: LOCVS QVO EA STRVES CONGERANTVR, i. e. piles of wood, Cenot. Pis. I. (in ).—
In partic., in relig. lang., a heap of little offering-cakes: strues genera liborum sunt, digitorum conjunctorum non dissimilia, qui superjecta panicula in transversum continentur, Müll.; cf. id. s. v. ferctum, p. 85; cf. ; ; ; Inscr. Fratr. Arv. ap. Marin. p. 403.

la:noun:strabo.gloss: a man or woman with distorted eyes, a cross-eyed person, a person who frequently squints
senses: a man or woman with distorted eyes, a cross-eyed person, a person who frequently squints
la:noun:strabo.html:
străbo, ōnis, m. (collat. form stră-bōnus, i, ; v. also strabus), = στραβών.
Lit., that has oblique, distorted eyes, i. e. one who squints strongly, a squinter (class.): ecquos (deos) si non tam strabones, at paetulos esse arbitramur? * ; , ; .—
Trop., one who looks askance, i. e. an envious, jealous person (ante-class.), Lucil. ap. (Sat. Fragm. 27, 8); (opp. integris oculis).

la:noun:strepitus.html:
strĕpĭtus, ūs (
gen. strepiti, Enn. ap. ; or Trag. v. 205 Vahl.), m.
strepo
.
Lit., a (wild, confused) noise, din of any kind; a clashing, crashing, rustling, rattling, clattering, clanking, rumbling, etc. (class. and very freq.; cf.: crepitus, stridor, fragor): strepitus, fremitus, clamor tonitruum, Poët. ap. ; cf.: strepitus, crepitus, sonitus, tonitrus,: molarum strepitus, Enn. ap. (Com. v. 7 Vahl.): fluminum,: strepitu nullo clam reserare fores,; so, ingens valvarum,: audis quo strepitu janua remugiat,: rotarum,; : obscenus, i. e. ventris, et saep.: comitum conventus, strepitus, clamor mulierum Fecere, ut, etc., prol. alt. 27: non strepitu, sed maximo clamore, (cf. ): inde fragore gravi strepitus loca terret,: prae strepitu et clamore,: magno cum strepitu ac tumultu castris egressi,; so (with tumultus) ; : concursus hominum forique strepitus,: Romae,: inter strepitum tot bellorum,; cf.: sententiarum vanissimus strepitus,.—In plur.: canis, sollicitum animal ad nocturnos strepitus,: vino, strepitibus clamoribusque nocturnis attoniti,.—
Poet., transf., a (measured, regular) sound: citharae,: testudinis aureae,: tibicinae,.

senses: to rattle, rustle, rumble, murmur, hum, roar
la:verb:strepo.html:
strĕpo, ui, 3, v. n. and a.
Neutr.
Lit., to make a noise; to rattle, rustle, rumble, murmur, hum, roar, etc. (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose; syn.: fremo, strideo): cum Achivi coepissent Inter se strepere, * Cic. poët. Div. 1, 16, 29: vocibus truculentis,: apes in alvo strepunt,; cf. .—Of musical instruments (poet.): rauco strepuerunt cornua cantu,; so, litui,: fluvii strepunt Hibernā nive turgidi,.—Of arms, etc.: strepit assiduo cava tempora circum Tinnitu galea,: lancea,: tonitrua,.— Of the place in which the sound is heard: strepit omnis murmure campus,: omnia terrore ac tumultu,; cf. : urbs apparatu belli,; cf. : aures clamoribus plorantium,: placidum aequor mille navium, remis,: armorum paratu provinciae,: mons tibiarum cantu tympanorumque sonitu,.—
Trop.: Scythici equitatūs equorum gloriā strepunt,ring, resound with the glory,: intra Albanam arcem sententia Messalini strepebat,i. e. was not heard beyond,.—
Act. (very rare): haec cum sub ipso vallo portisque streperent,bawled out, vociferated,: strepens immania,making strenuous accusations,: qui (lucus) Capitolium montem strepit,fills with rustling,.

la:noun:structor.html:
structor, ōris, m.
id.
.
One who erects a building, a builder, mason, carpenter: res agebatur multis structoribus,; ; ; ; ; —
One who spreads the table or serves up food and carves; a server, carver (post-Aug.): ferculorum compositor, Serv. ap. ; ; ; ; .—
Trop.: orationis,.

la:adj:strenuus.html:
strēnuus, a, um, adj.
root in Gr. στερεός, firm, hard; cf. sterilis, and Germ. starren
,
brisk, nimble, quick, prompt, active, vigorous, strenuous.
Of persons (freq. and class.; syn.: fortis, alacer, agilis): mercator strenuus, Cato, R. R. praef. § 3; cf.: vilicus strenuior, Lucil. ap. P. (Sat. 16, 5): strenui nimio plus prosunt populi quam arguti et cati,: homo,: multi alii ex Trojā strenui viri,: strenuior (opp. deterior),: viri fortissimi et milites strenuissimi, Cato, R. R. praef. § 4; cf. : strenuus et fortis,; : imperator in proeliis strenuus et fortis,: strenui ignavique in victoriā idem audent,; so (opp. ignavus) ; (opp. iners) ; ; : noli me tam strenuum putare, ut ad Nonas recurram, Hirt. ap. : Graeci, gens linguā magis strenua quam factis,; : quodsi cessas aut strenuus anteis, et saep.—With gen.: strenuus militiae,.—
Restless, turbulent (post-Aug.): multi in utroque exercitu, sicut modesti quietique, ita mali et strenui,: strenuus in perfidiā,.—
Transf., of things (not in class. prose): operam reipublicae fortem atque strenuam perhibere, Cato ap. ; cf. : adulescens strenuā facie,: manus (chirurgi),nimble, quick, dexterous,med.: corpus,: navis,: strenua nos exercet inertia,busy idleness,: transiliebant in vehicula strenuo saltu,: toxica,quick, speedy,: remedium,: causa tam strenuae mortis,.—Hence, adv.: strē-nuē, briskly, quickly, promptly, actively, strenuously: strenue quod volumus ostendere factum, celeriuscule dicemus, at aliud otiose, retardabimus,: aliquid facere,: converrite scopis, agite strenue, id. Fragm. ap. P.: abi prae strenue ac aperi fores,: arma capere,: aedificare domum,: praesto fuit sane strenue,.—Without a verb: Da. Jam hercle ego illum nominabo. Tr. Euge strenue, ; .— Sup.: per hos strenuissime omnia bella confecta,.—Comp. seems not to occur.

la:verb:strangulo.html:
strangŭlo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., = στραγγαλάω (cf. Müll.),
to throttle, choke; and, in gen., to stifle, suffocate, strangle (syn. suffoco).
Lit. (class.): Domitium strangulavit, Cael. ap. : strangulata laqueo,: strangulatus in carcere,; : venena quae strangulando necant,: obesi difficultate spirandi strangulantur,: piro strangulatus,: strangulatae in oleo ranae,: cuniculos vapore,: ne nimio sanguine stranguletur pecus,; : volvam strangulati,: sinus (togae) nec strangulet nec fluat,too closely drawn together,.—In an obscene double sense: si dicimus, Ille patrem strangulavit, honorem non praefamur. Sin de Aureliā aliquid aut Lolliā, honos praefandus est, * . —
Transf., of things: hedera arbores sugit et strangulat, chokes, i. e. kills, makes unfruitful, : truncum,: sata,: solum,: fauces tumentes strangulant vocem,choke, stifle, constrain,; so, sonitum,.—Poet.: non tibi sepositas infelix strangulat arca Divitias,i. e. contains,.—
Trop., to torment, torture (poet. and in post-class. prose): strangulat inclusus dolor atque exaestuat intus,: voluptates in hoc nos amplectuntur, ut strangulent,: plures nimiā congesta pecunia curā Strangulat,: venditor omnes causas, quibus strangulatur, exponat, i. e. is forced to the sale, Cod. Th. 12, 3, 1.

la:noun:stridor.gloss: a harsh, shrill, hissing, grating, or creaking sound
senses: a harsh, shrill, hissing, grating, or creaking sound
la:noun:stridor.html:
strīdor, ōris, m.
strideo
,
any harsh, shrill, hissing, grating, or creaking sound; a creaking, hissing, rattling, buzzing, whizzing, whistling, etc. (class.; esp. freq. in the poets; cf.: strepitus, clangor): serpentis,; cf. : elephantorum, ; ; ; : stellionis,: simiae,: volant pinnarum stridore (locustae),: Troglodytis stridor, non vox,: horrifer Aquiloni' stridor, Att. ap. (Trag. Rel. v. 567 Rib.): ne stridorem quidem serrae, cum acuitur (audiunt),; id. poët. Div. 1, 7, 13: procellae, (4, 6), 47: rudentum,; : januae,: dentium,; : pinnarum,: lituum,: catenae,: harena, quae manu confricata fecerit stridorem, et saep.: tribuni plebis stridor,: stridor acutus,; ; : consonantium tristior stridor,.—Plur.: stridores aurium,.

la:verb:strido.gloss: to utter or make a shrill or harsh sound; creak, shriek, squeak, screech, grate, hiss, whistle, buzz
senses: to utter or make a shrill or harsh sound; creak, shriek, squeak, screech, grate, hiss, whistle, buzz

la:verb:strideo.gloss: to utter or make a shrill or harsh sound; creak, shriek, squeak, screech, grate, hiss, whistle, buzz
senses: alternative form of strīdō ("utter or make a shrill or harsh sound")
la:verb:strideo.html:
strīdeo, di, 2, and strīdo, di, 3 (both forms equally in use;
v.in the foll.) [perh. root star, to resound; cf. Gr. τρίζω, τόργος; also Lat. turdus, sterto, trisso], v. n., to make or utter any harsh, shrill, hissing, whistling, grating, or creaking sound; to creak, hiss, whizz, whistle, rattle, buzz (mostly poet.; cf.: strepo, fremo): ferri stridit acumen, Enn. ap. P. (Ann. v. 364 Vahl.): striderat hasta, p. 817 P. (Ann. v. 365 Vahl.): candens ferrum e fornacibus Stridit,; cf. ; ; : striduntque cavernis Stricturae chalybum,: serpentum Cerberus ore Stridet,; cf. : striges,: gryllus,: barbaraque horribili stridebat tibia cantu,: serrae stridentis acerbus Horror,: foribus cardo aënis,: plaustra,: mare refluentibus undis,: alae cygnorum,: sagitta,; cf. : silvae,: rudentes aquilone,: aeger dentibus stridet,: jecur in verubus,: funes,.—With human subjects, of any loud or inharmonious sound: quidnam hoc soniti est, quod stridunt foris? Pac. ap. (Trag. Rel. v. 133 Rib.). cum striderat (Alcestis) retracta rursus inferis, Att. ap. P. (Trag. Rel. v. 57 Rib.): Troglodytae stridunt magis quam loquuntur,: stridunt animae currumque sequuntur,: pressoque diu stridere molari,gnash,.

la:verb:stringo.gloss: to draw tight together, to tie together
senses: to draw tight together, to tie together
to pull or strip off, cut off, pluck off, clip off, prune
to touch lightly, graze, wound slightly
la:verb:stringo.html:
stringo, inxi, ictum, 3, v. a.
root strig; Gr. στραγγ-, to squeeze; στράγξ, a drop; cf. O. H. Germ. streng; Engl. strong
,
to draw tight, to bind or tie tight; to draw, bind, or press together, etc. (syn. ligo).
Lit.: te stringam ad carnarium,: stringit vitta comas,: caesariem crinali cultu, Claud. Cons. Prob. et Olybr. 85: stricta matutino frigore vulnera,: pectora pigro gelu,: strictos insedimus amnes,: mare gelu stringi et consistere,: quercus in duas partes diducta, stricta denuo et cohaesa,having closed together,: habenam,to draw tight,: ferrum,.—
Transf. (through the intermediate idea of drawing close), to touch, touch upon, touch lightly or slightly, to graze (syn. tango): litus ama, et laevas stringat sine palmula cautes,; cf.: stringebat summas ales miserabilis undas,: aequor (aurā),: metas interiore rotā,: latus, (4, 10), 24: vestigia canis rostro, et saep.: equos,to stroke, P.: tela stringentia corpus,i. e. slightly touching,; cf. : coluber Dente pedem strinxit,: strictus ac recreatus ex vulnere in tempus,.—
To pull or strip off, to pluck off, cut off, clip off, prune, etc. (cf. destringo): oleam ubi nigra erit, stringito,; so, oleam,: bacam,: quernas glandes,: folia ex arboribus,; : frondes,; : hordea,: arbores,: celeriter gladios strinxerunt,drew from the sheath, unsheathed,: strictam aciem offerre,: ensem,; so, gladios,; : ensem,; 14, 296: ferrum,: cultrum,; ; and poet. transf.: manum,to bare,; —
Trop.
Of speech, to touch upon, treat briefly, .—Hence, to compress, abridge: narrationis loco rem stringat, Spald.—
To hold in check, to rule, sway (syn. coërceo): quaecumque meo gens barbara nutu Stringitur, adveniat,.—
To waste, consume, reduce: praeclaram stringat malus ingluvie rem,.—
(Acc. to I. B.) To touch, move, affect; esp. to affect painfully, to wound, pain: atque animum patriae strinxit pietatis imago,: quam tua delicto stringantur pectora nostro,: nomen alicujus,.—
To draw in hostility, attack with: in hostes stringatur iambus,: bellum,.—Hence, strictus, a, um, P. a. (acc. to I.), drawn together, close, strait, tight, etc.
Lit.: laxaret pedem a stricto nodo,: duriora genti corpora, stricti artus,: strictissima janua,: si strictior fuerit pedatura,: emplastrum,thick,: venter,i. e. bound up, costive,: strictior aura,more severe, colder,.—
Trop.
Of language, brief, concise: quo minus (Aeschines) strictus est,: qui (Demosthenes) est strictior multo (quam Cicero),.—
Of character, severe, strict: Catones,: mentes,: lex,.—
Rigid, exact (law Lat.): restitutio stricto jure non competebat,; —Adv.: strictē and strictim, closely, tightly: in foramen conicies,.—Comp., .—Sup., .—
Fig., accurately: strictius interpretari,.

senses: Two small islands of the Ionian Sea

Strŏphădes, um, f., = Στροφἀδες,
two islands lying off the coast of Messenia, at first called Plotœ, celebrated as the fabled residence of the Harpies, now Strofahia, ; ; ; ; .

la:noun:strages.html:
strāges, is, f.
sterno, II. B.
,
a throwing down, throwing to the ground, overthrowing; an overthrow; confusion, confused heap or mass (cf.: acervus, strues; not freq. till after the Aug. per., esp. in Liv.; not in Cæs.).
Lit.
In gen.
With gen.: strage armorum saepta via est,: nemorum,: ruinae,: minarum,: aedificiorum et hominum,: obstantis molis,: rerum in trepidatione nocturna passim relictarum,: boum hominumque,: canum volucrumque aviumque boumque,: exercituum,, ext. 1.—
Absol.: dabit ille (nimbus) ruinas Arboribus stragemque satis,: atrox tempestas multis locis stragem fecit,: strage ac ruinā fudere Gallos,; cf. .—
Pregn., a mortal overthrow; a defeat, slaughter, massacre, butchery, carnage (syn.: caedes, clades): stragem horribilem caedemque vereri, Cic. poët. Div. 1, 12, 20; so (with caedes) ; ; Val. Max. 5, 6, 5; cf.: quantas acies stragemque ciebunt!: confusae stragis acervus,: complere strage campos,.—In plur.: strages facere,: strages edere,; ; ; ; ; cf. also II.: cruentae,.—*
Trop., overthrow, ruin, destruction: quas ego pugnas et quantas strages edidi!.

la:noun:structura.gloss: the practice or process of building, construction
senses: the practice or process of building, construction
the method, form, structure or arrangement of anything
masonry, brickwork; cement (the result of application of a certain construction technique)
la:noun:structura.html:
structūra, ae, f.
struo
,
a fitting together, adaptation, adjustment.
Lit.
In gen. (post-Aug. and very rare): ossa in manu oblonga omnia et triangula, structurā quādam inter se conectuntur,: membranarum,: togae,.—
In partic., an architectural fitting together, a building or erecting.
In abstr. (class.): parietum, the mode of building, construction, * ; cf.: structurae antiquae genus,; and: reticulata structura,: (silex) globosus sed structurae infidelis,for building,: in structurā saxorum rudium,.—Plur.: in structuris lapidum impolitorum,.—

Trop., of language, an arrangement, order, structure (in Cic. only as a figure of speech, with quasi or quaedam; later in gen.): verborum quasi structura,: quasi structura quaedam,: et verborum est structura quaedam,: proprietates verborum exigit, et structuram et argumentationes,: mei carminis,; ; ; ; 9, 4, 45;
